# Studyflow: a BPMN-based notation, modeler, and runner for end-to-end specification of experimental research workflows in cognitive sciences

**Authors:**
Morteza Ansarinia^1,\*^ (ORCID 0000-0001-8335-6704),
Hoorieh Afkari Roshan^1^ (ORCID 0000-0003-4787-8331),
Pedro Cardoso-Leite^1^ (ORCID 0000-0002-2848-5527)

^1^ University of Luxembourg, Luxembourg
^\*^ Corresponding author: morteza.ansarinia@uni.lu

## Abstract

A scientific study passes through many hands: researcher, ethics reviewer, participant, data engineer, analyst, reviewer, replicator; and each typically receives a different artifact: a protocol PDF, an experiment script, a preprocessing notebook, a manuscript figure, a CONSORT diagram. These artifacts drift apart, and no single representation describes the study as it was actually run. We present **Studyflow**, a notation that closes this gap by extending Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) with elements specific to experimental cognitive science: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization and eligibility), data operations (map, filter, reduce, group), and data elements bound to community schemas (BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, CSVW). A single `.studyflow` file serves as protocol, specification, publication figure, and participant-facing application. We describe the language, an open-source modeler, and a client-side runner, and demonstrate end-to-end use on a CONSORT-style trial, an N-back task, and a reproducible analysis pipeline.

## Impact statement

Studyflow turns a scientific study into a single source-of-truth diagram that can be reviewed, executed, and published, replacing the divergent artifacts (protocols, scripts, pipeline parameters, reporting diagrams) that currently fragment experimental research across stakeholders.

## Keywords

scientific workflows; experimental design; BPMN; reproducibility; process modeling

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

A scientific study touches many people and systems. A researcher designs it; an ethics reviewer approves it; a participant runs it; a data pipeline ingests it; a model trains on it; a reviewer reads it in a manuscript; a replicator tries to rebuild it. Reproducing the study after the fact requires more than the data and the manuscript: it requires an explicit, complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. A complete description of any computing system needs both a data model and a process model [@Sehgal2011]; in the life sciences and cognitive sciences, however, most standardization effort has gone into data, leaving the processes that produce the data documented in narrative prose, ad-hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories that drift apart from the prose they accompany [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015].

The cost of this asymmetry is visible whenever a study has to be re-read by anyone other than its author. The researcher's protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card, the manuscript figure, and the CONSORT diagram begin as different views of the same study and end as inconsistent ones. By the end, no single thing describes the study *as it was actually run*. Trust in research, and increasingly trust in code and data on which research depends, is built or lost at exactly that junction.

The mechanism most often used against this asymmetry is voluntary, narrative reporting (checklists, pre-registration forms, journal endorsements), and the empirical record on whether it works is now available. A cross-sectional study of 400 psychology articles published in 2022 found that only 7%-14% had been preregistered and only 14%-16% shared raw data, despite more than a decade of reform initiatives [@hardwicke2024prevalence]. The pattern is not limited to psychology: ARRIVE 2.0 explicitly documents that endorsement by more than 1000 journals failed to improve adherence, and a randomized trial at *PLOS ONE* found that requesting a completed checklist at submission did not improve disclosure either [@percie2020arrive]. Even at journals that have moved transparency from opt-in to default policy, the shift required explicit editorial mandates rather than voluntary uptake [@hardwicke2024transparency]. The conclusion is not that researchers are uncooperative but that narrative checklists are the wrong instrument: they specify *what to mention* in prose without requiring *what to actually share*, as they accept a narrative description of the study workflow in place of a formal, verifiable one. They leave the underlying process model implicit.

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact itself rather than a separate documentation effort maintained alongside the work. A single, machine-readable, human-understandable representation of a study, shared across its audiences, would force the process model and the data model to stay aligned. The contribution of this paper is one concrete realization of that idea, grounded in a standard process notation and a working open source toolset.

## 1.2 Current practice fragments the study across artifacts

Today, the audiences of science listed above each receive a different artifact, and each artifact drifts from the others. We can sort current approaches into four overlapping families.

**Box-and-arrow figures** in manuscripts and protocols communicate study logic at a glance but are not standardized, not machine-checkable, and rarely connect to the code that runs the study. They are tailored to each stakeholder (a CONSORT flow for a journal, a slide deck for a funder, a sketch on a whiteboard for an engineer) and so are difficult to keep mutually consistent [@visualmodelinglanguagesscopingreview]. **Checklists and pre-registration forms**, cataloged at scale through the EQUATOR network [@simera2010equator], address the need for structured text but encode it in free-form fields, in proprietary PDF or DOCX, on data silos that resist version control [@barrowman2020vtree]. **Data standards, ontologies, and packages** (BIDS, Psych-DS, the Behaverse Data Model, CSVW [@bids; @psychds; @bdm; @csvw]) make the data side machine-readable but say little about the procedure that produced the data, and ontology-based process models, while numerous, demand high upfront effort and are rarely reused [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. **Code and configuration** (analysis scripts, GitHub Actions, Nextflow [@kinsman2021], protocol registries such as protocols.io [@teytelman2016]) make pipelines precise but require programming literacy that excludes ethics boards, reviewers, and many collaborators.

The recurring pattern is a split between **execution** and **communication**: tools that execute the study (scripts, workflow engines, CI pipelines) target developers and machines; tools that communicate the study (protocol PDFs, narrative platforms, reporting checklists) target humans. Provenance systems track the computational graph well but rarely capture the full experimental context — randomization decisions, manual annotations, protocol deviations — creating a boundary between a well-tracked computational graph and a partially represented experimental graph [@souza2020provenance; @simmons2018provenance_sport]. No single representation currently spans the full lifecycle of a study in a form that scientists, engineers, ethics boards, and journal editors can all read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## 1.3 BPMN as a foundation

The domain (designing, executing, and reporting experiments in cognitive sciences) meets the standard criteria for building a domain-specific modeling language (DSML): recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general-purpose code, and the absence of an executable specification language that already covers the lifecycle end-to-end [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new graphical language for cognitive experiments, we extend an established one whose visual conventions have already paid the cognitive-effectiveness cost of adoption. The principles that distinguish an effective visual notation from a merely correct one are themselves a research subject [@moody2009physics], and a notation that researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize is the cheaper starting point.

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature ISO-standard graphical language for processes [@white2004introduction]. It already provides what scientific workflows need at the structural level: events, activities, sub-processes, exclusive/parallel/inclusive gateways, data objects and stores, sequence and message flows, and choreography between participants. It has an established tooling ecosystem (editors and renderers such as `bpmn-js` and Camunda Modeler, drawing libraries such as diagrams.net) and a body of accumulated practice in industries where process clarity is not optional. Building on BPMN gives any domain-specific extension a shape vocabulary that engineers and analysts already recognize, plus a serialization (BPMN 2.0 XML) that survives outside any single tool.

BPMN's extension mechanism — `extensionElements` and namespaced attributes — is the bridge we use. The standard permits domain-specific elements and attributes to be added inside a vendor namespace; a BPMN-only parser ignores them gracefully, while a domain-aware tool can validate and render them [@magnani2009bpdmn]. Existing BPMN extensions in adjacent domains demonstrate the pattern: BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless machine-learning pipelines [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], extensions for human-AI collaboration [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent], and applications to healthcare more broadly [@pufahl2022]. A systematic review identifies dozens more profiles across domains [@zarour2019], and a complementary taxonomy classifies how such extensions relate to the BPMN core [@braun2014classification]. Cognitive and behavioural research is conspicuously absent from this list.

Recent large-language-model-assisted BPMN authoring tools (ProMoAI, BPMN-ChatBot, and related work [@kourani2024promoai; @kourani2024process_modeling_llm]) accelerate diagram authoring from text, but evaluations show that competitive syntactic quality does not translate into domain-specific semantics or domain-specific validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Authoring help is welcome; it is not a substitute for a profile that defines what *cognitive task*, *random assignment*, or *eligibility check* mean inside a process model. That profile is the gap Studyflow fills.

## 1.4 Contributions and roadmap

We contribute five artifacts, each independently usable:

1. **A versioned language specification** for Studyflow, authored as a LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that serves as the single source of truth for element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules. LinkML is a schema-modeling framework increasingly adopted across biology, biomedicine, and ontology engineering, and provides FAIR-aligned [@fair] serialization plus tooling for documentation, validator, and downstream-converter generation. The Studyflow LinkML schema is independent of any particular implementation: a third party can target it directly without depending on the modeler's code.

2. **A layered set of runtime schemas** mirroring the LinkML specification in the YAML format that BPMN tooling consumes — comprising the language core, a companion cognitive layer, and four optional domain extensions (Behaverse cognitive battery, generic process orchestration, large-scale data transformation, multimodal acquisition). New domain semantics plug in without touching the core.

3. **A library of worked example diagrams** that ship with the modeler, including a 423-line CONSORT-2025 randomized trial, a 378-line SPIRIT-2025 protocol schedule, and patterns for cognitive tasks, data collection, analysis pipelines, MLOps, multi-agent choreography, and reporting guidelines.

4. **The Studyflow Modeler**, an open-source client-side web application (MIT-licensed) for authoring, inspecting, simulating, validating, and publishing Studyflow diagrams. Its inspector and palette are generated from the schemas, so the language and the editor stay in sync.

5. **The Studyflow Runner**, a separate client-side application that parses, validates, and walks a Studyflow file step by step. It ships with built-in renderers for consents, instructions, questionnaire instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II), generic tasks, and embedded Behaverse cognitive-task runtimes; supports seeded determinism for reproducible random branches; and drives human participants, classic agents (via CogEnv), and language-model agents from the same diagram (§2.12).

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. §2 describes the language, modeler, and runner, and demonstrates them end-to-end on a CONSORT-style randomized controlled trial (§2.5), an N-back cognitive task authored, published, and run on the runner (§2.6), and a reproducible reaction-time analysis pipeline (§2.7). §2 also examines how Studyflow covers existing reporting guidelines (§2.8), how process and data fit in one diagram (§2.9), how MLOps workflows can be expressed in the same notation (§2.10), how multi-agent studies are modelled via BPMN choreography (§2.11), and how the same Studyflow source drives three different runtime executions — human, classic RL agent, and LLM agent (§2.12). §3 discusses what Studyflow changes for the field, its relationship to neighbouring ecosystems, and directions for community-led extension. A closing *Code and data availability* section lists the open-source artifacts and links to the canonical LinkML specification.

# 2. Results

§2 is organized in three movements. The first (§2.1-§2.4) describes Studyflow's working artifacts — the language, the modeler, and the runner — together with the three rendering views (Study, Gantt, Checklist) that let one source file serve readers with different needs. The second (§2.5-§2.7) demonstrates the language end-to-end on three workflows: a CONSORT-style randomized controlled trial, an N-back cognitive task authored, published, and run on the runner, and a reproducible reaction-time analysis pipeline. The third (§2.8-§2.12) maps Studyflow onto adjacent territory: coverage of reporting guidelines beyond CONSORT, the integration of process and data in one diagram, the application to MLOps workflows, multi-agent studies via BPMN choreography, and the same diagram driving three distinct runtime executions (human, classic RL agent, LLM agent).

## 2.1 The Studyflow language

Studyflow is a domain-specific profile of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0 [@white2004introduction] tailored to experimental research in cognitive sciences. We adopted BPMN as the host notation rather than inventing a new language for three reasons. First, Studyflow diagrams remain valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool (Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io, diagrams.net), with Studyflow-specific elements degrading gracefully. Second, BPMN's flowchart-like visual grammar is already familiar to many researchers, lowering adoption barriers; readers without prior flowchart exposure still face a small learning curve, but a shallower one than a custom domain-specific language would impose. Third, BPMN provides a formal extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) for adding domain semantics without breaking the base standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn].

**What Studyflow inherits.** Studyflow reuses BPMN's full vocabulary for control flow and structure: start, end, intermediate, boundary, timer, and error *events*; tasks, sub-processes, and call activities; exclusive, parallel, inclusive, event-based, and complex *gateways*; sequence flows and message flows; data objects and data stores with their associations; pools and lanes; and choreography for multi-agent interactions. These elements render with standard BPMN shapes and behave exactly as specified by the OMG.

**What Studyflow adds.** Four areas extend BPMN with vocabulary that experimental research routinely needs. First, a top-level **study container** groups every other element and carries study-level metadata (title, version, authors, runtime). Second, **domain-specific activity types** specialize the generic BPMN task with research-meaningful kinds — cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest periods, video games, and the curated Behaverse cognitive battery — each rendering with a distinctive icon while remaining a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, **research-specific data elements** augment BPMN's generic data objects with bindings to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], the Behaverse Data Model, CSVW), and a small **data-operations vocabulary** (map, filter, reduce, group, transform, compose) renders the *kind* of transformation as a task marker, so how data flows is visible at a glance. Fourth, **research gateways** encode the branching patterns specific to experimental design: a random gateway for randomization, a stratified-allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria. Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attached to activities and events let the Gantt view derive trial schedules and visit calendars from the same diagram (§2.4).

**What Studyflow deliberately leaves alone.** Studyflow does not redefine BPMN's serialization conventions: XML namespaces, element identifiers, and the base shape vocabulary are untouched. Domain extensions live inside BPMN's native extension slot, so a generic BPMN renderer ignores them gracefully while a Studyflow-aware tool validates and renders them consistently.

**A layered set of schemas.** The vocabulary is partitioned into a small core and optional domain extensions that can be loaded on demand (Figure 2). The core covers the language scaffolding (study container, events, sequence flows, base activity, data infrastructure) plus a companion cognitive layer (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest, video games, research gateways). Four optional layers cover specific domains — the Behaverse Unity battery, generic process orchestration, large-scale data transformation, and multimodal acquisition for EEG and eye tracking — and new domains plug in by authoring a schema without modifying the core. The complete element catalog is provided in Supplementary Table S1.

## 2.2 The Studyflow Modeler

The **Studyflow Modeler** is an open-source web application (MIT-licensed) that operationalizes the Studyflow language for authoring, inspecting, simulating, and publishing diagrams. It is a client-side application without a server dependency, continuously deployed at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/>. Two design choices shape the modeler. First, the language specification is maintained as a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] independent of the modeler codebase, so third-party tools (linters, converters, execution engines) can target the same specification. The modeler tracks the schema rather than owning it. Second, the user interface is **schema-driven**: palette entries, the inspector panel, and validation rules are generated from the layered moddle schemas (§2.1). Adding an element type or attribute to a schema updates the UI without manual UI work, which has so far kept the modeler lightweight while the notation evolves with community feedback.

The authoring workflow (Figure 3) proceeds in seven steps. (1) **Sign in.** Users open the hosted modeler. A Behaverse API key unlocks publish; guest mode supports draft-only authoring. (2) **Drag from the palette.** The left palette exposes the BPMN base vocabulary alongside the Studyflow-specific elements (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction, random gateway, eligibility gateway, dataset, etc.); optional schemas can be toggled from the palette settings. (3) **Edit in the inspector.** Selecting an element opens a right-hand inspector sidebar whose fields are derived from the element's schema entry: required attributes are flagged, enumerated values become dropdowns, markdown fields render with a preview, and conditional attributes appear only when their predicate holds. (4) **Connect elements.** The connect tool wires sequence flows, data associations, and message flows; the modeler picks the appropriate edge type from the source/target pair. (5) **Save and export.** Diagrams persist as `.studyflow` files — BPMN 2.0 XML with Studyflow extensions in named namespaces — so they diff cleanly in Git and remain valid BPMN. Export to PNG and SVG produces publication-ready figures; SVGs can embed the source XML for one-file commits. (6) **Simulate.** A simulation mode steps through the diagram interactively, exercising gateway logic and showing the next admissible elements, which is useful for catching dead branches and missing conditions before a study runs. (7) **Publish.** *File → Publish* uploads the diagram to the Behaverse Data Server [@bds], which renders its own participant-facing UI from the diagram structure (local layout in the modeler is for human readers; the server ignores it). Local stimuli must be referenced by URL or uploaded separately. Each publish creates a new server-side version, so studies already in the field do not break when authors push updates, and earlier versions remain reachable by identifier.

This separation between specification (the LinkML schema), authoring tool (the modeler), runtime UI (the data server), and visual layout (export artifacts) lets each component evolve independently while a single `.studyflow` source ties them together.

## 2.3 The Studyflow Runner

The **Studyflow Runner** is a distinct client-side application that takes a Studyflow diagram and walks a participant — or an artificial agent (§2.12) — through it node by node. It lives alongside the modeler. A diagram reaches it three ways: from the modeler's *Run* button, by URL parameter when the diagram is hosted somewhere, or by direct file upload. An optional random seed makes any branching deterministic, so pilot runs and regression tests are reproducible.

After loading, the runner parses the diagram, validates it node by node, and traverses it from start to end. Validation is layered: type-level constraints (required attributes, enumerated values, conditional visibility) are checked at parse time; structural constraints (every start has an outgoing flow, every gateway is fully wired, every flow has a valid source and target) are checked by the modeler at edit time; per-step validators (a questionnaire needs an instrument, a Behaverse cognitive task needs a paradigm identifier) run before traversal begins. The same per-step validators are exposed to the modeler's lint pass, so authors see the errors they would see at run time. Each visited node yields a step that the runner renders and waits to complete; when the end event is reached, the run finishes and any completion code or redirect specified in the diagram takes effect.

**Gateway semantics.** Random gateways select an outgoing branch uniformly at random under the seed. Stratified allocation currently falls back to the same uniform pick; balanced stratification is roadmap work. Exclusive and inclusive gateways evaluate conditions against a runtime variable store that nodes can write to as they execute, with fallback to a default branch when no condition matches. Parallel gateways are not yet supported.

**Built-in step kinds.** Six kinds ship: a **start** node that shows a consent screen when one is attached, an **end** node that issues a completion code and an optional redirect, an **instruction** node that renders markdown, a **questionnaire** node with built-in instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II) plus custom instruments via inline schema, a **Behaverse cognitive-task** node that embeds the Behaverse Unity runtime and supports three response sources — Unity's in-game bot, runner-side uniform random, or a language-model call per trial (§2.12) — and a **generic-task** fallback. Element kinds that are not steps in the participant flow (data references, model-only sub-processes) are skipped at run time — they affect modeling and analysis, not execution.

**Runtime extensibility.** New step kinds plug in by adding one folder to the runner's node directory: a small matcher selects which diagram elements the kind handles, a mapper extracts the runtime parameters from the element, and a React component renders the step. A domain group can thus ship a custom step — an eye-tracking calibration, a VR scene — without forking the runner. The runner's curated step set, absent parallel-gateway support, and the stratified-allocation fallback to uniform random are scope choices rather than language limitations: the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time, and each gap maps to a roadmap item (§3.3).

Figure 4 [GAP: a four-to-six-panel walkthrough of a participant moving from consent through an instruction, a questionnaire, and a Behaverse cognitive task to the end screen, on the same diagram authored in §2.2.]

## 2.4 The three views: Study / Gantt / Checklist

A single `.studyflow` source is rendered three ways, each tuned to a different stakeholder need (Figure 5). The three views read the same file, so changes propagate automatically.

**Study view.** The default rendering: a BPMN-like graph showing every element and connection. The Study view is *structural* — it shows what happens and in what order but does not commit to wall-clock timing. It is the canonical view for Methods sections, for reviewers checking logical structure, and for pipeline authors wiring up data flow.

**Gantt view.** A Gantt-style rendering that places time-sensitive elements along a temporal axis. BPMN has timer events but no native way to express activity duration, scheduled onset, or progress. Studyflow attaches these as optional attributes on BPMN activities and events: **onset**, **duration**, and **progress** (percentage or label). Resource allocation is expressed directly as BPMN pools and lanes, which the Gantt uses to group rows — there is no separate `resourceAllocation` attribute. When the temporal attributes are present, the Gantt view renders the diagram automatically. The same mechanism scales from trial-level timing (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to study-level timing (visit schedule, follow-ups). Milestones are the special case of zero duration, and hierarchical Gantt structures map directly onto BPMN sub-processes. The Gantt view is particularly useful for longitudinal studies and SPIRIT-style schedules of enrolment and assessment [@spirit2013].

**Checklist view.** A task-oriented view that flattens the diagram into a list of activities with their associated items and status. Every Studyflow element carries an optional `checklist` attribute — a markdown list — that the Checklist view extracts and aggregates. The view supports two uses: *running studies day-to-day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, CARE), where guideline items are mapped to the diagram elements that satisfy them so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. Checklists ship with the `.studyflow` file and can be exported to JSON or Markdown for external task managers (§2.8 returns to reporting-guideline coverage).

| If you need to communicate... | Use |
|---|---|
| Procedural structure, branching, data flow | Study view |
| Wall-clock timing, schedules, durations | Gantt view |
| Coverage against a reporting checklist or protocol | Checklist view |

A single `.studyflow` source thus underwrites three reading paths — a methods diagram, a project schedule, a reporting audit — without forcing authors to maintain three artifacts that drift apart.


## 2.5 Demonstration I — CONSORT-style randomized controlled trial

CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) prescribes a checklist plus a flow diagram for documenting randomized controlled trials [@moher2012; @rennie2001]. The flow diagram, in particular, is a participant-tracking schematic with enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and analysis as the four canonical rows, and with attrition counts annotating each transition. In current practice this diagram is drawn at write-up time, typically in a presentation or drawing program, and bears no machine-readable connection to the protocol that was registered, to the data collection system that recruited the participants, or to the analysis code that produced the published estimates. The diagram is a *document* about the trial, not the *spec* that drove it.

Studyflow inverts this relationship. We ship a 423-line CONSORT 2025 reference diagram (`src/assets/examples/consort2025.studyflow`) that authors can fork, parameterize, and run as the actual protocol of a new trial. Figure 6 contrasts three artifacts: (a) the canonical CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated comparison whose left path uses Studyflow boundary error events and whose right path uses the traditional text-and-box treatment.

The crucial mechanical difference is how attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box is an unconnected annotation sitting next to the column of follow-up activities; readers infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the Studyflow diagram, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity from which participants departed. Exclusion at screening hangs off the eligibility gateway; non-receipt of intervention off the two allocation tasks; loss to follow-up and discontinuation off the follow-up tasks; exclusion from analysis off the analysis tasks. Each event terminates in an error end event with a labeled count. This has three consequences. The topology of the diagram now matches the topology of the trial: a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge whose origin is the follow-up activity itself, not along an arrow drawn from a side annotation. Summing attrition becomes a graph operation rather than a manual exercise — a Studyflow-aware validator can verify that no row's outbound counts exceed its inbound count. And the boundary error event is the same primitive BPMN uses to model interrupts in any business process, so the diagram remains valid BPMN 2.0 and inherits the standard execution semantics for error handling [@stroppi2011; @ait2024bpmn_humanagent].

The shipped CONSORT diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN scaffolding. The enrollment start event references a participant-facing consent PDF, so a runner that hits this node renders the consent screen automatically before any randomization happens. The screening task carries a markdown checklist (demographic intake, medical history, vital signs, baseline cognitive screen) that also drives the Checklist view (§2.4). The eligibility gateway and the randomization gateway are typed as such, and the follow-up tasks declare themselves as cognitive tasks with an instrument hint (jsPsych) and an inline parameter block (n-back duration, n-back levels, trials per block). Allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks each carry their own checklists describing protocol obligations.

This means a single Studyflow file simultaneously serves four readers. The trial registry sees a registered protocol with explicit randomization and eligibility criteria. The ethics board sees the consent screen content and the per-task checklists. The data collection platform sees the embedded cognitive-task instrument and parameters. The journal sees the CONSORT-compatible figure with attrition flows already wired. The mechanism that makes this work is not new — it is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011], with each reader interpreting the layer it cares about. What is new is that the union of these layers, rendered together, *is* a CONSORT diagram.

[GAP: coverage table mapping CONSORT 2025 items to machine-checked / encoded-as-attribute / author-discipline categories, derived by inspecting the 25-item CONSORT 2025 checklist against the shipping `consort2025.studyflow` artifact.]

The reverse direction is also supported: starting from a Studyflow file that already encodes the protocol, the modeler renders the CONSORT-style figure as a publication asset without any redrawing. The figure that appears in the paper is the file that ran the trial. We see this as one of the more direct responses to the "different artifacts drift" failure pattern described in §1.2.

## 2.6 Demonstration II — A cognitive task end-to-end: N-back

To validate the round-trip from authored diagram to running experiment, we walk through an N-back working-memory task encoded as a Studyflow. The N-back is a near-universal probe of working memory [@bell2021perspectives] and is normally documented as a slide-style schematic showing one or two example trials, annotated with stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and the target-match rule. The slide is intuitive but underdetermined: timing values often live only in the figure caption, the boundary between trial and block is implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in the analysis code. Figure 7 places the traditional slide-style figure next to the Studyflow equivalent.

The Studyflow N-back authors the trial as an explicit subgraph. Each trial begins with a stimulus activity; a boundary timer attached to that activity defines the response window (one second in our example); a second boundary timer encodes the inter-trial interval; text annotations on the response branches label them as target and non-target matches. The trial-by-trial encoding in Figure 7 is pedagogical; for execution beyond a handful of trials, the same logic compresses into a single Behaverse cognitive task whose inline configuration declares the N level, stream specification, trial count, stimulus duration, and inter-trial interval — and which the runner expands into individual trials via the Behaverse Unity runtime. Trials compose into a block, blocks loop until a counter reaches the target trial count, and the loop's exit edge transitions to the next block at a different N level. The XML excerpt in Figure 7c shows how these primitives serialize.

The empirical anchor of this section is the round-trip itself. We authored the N-back in the Studyflow Modeler (§2.2), saved it as a Studyflow diagram, then loaded that file into the Studyflow Runner (§2.3). The runner validates that every required parameter is present (response window, stimulus duration, N level, target rule) before traversal begins, then walks the diagram one node at a time. The N-back's elements are covered by the runner's built-in step kinds — instructions render as markdown, the questionnaire that precedes the task uses a built-in instrument (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II all ship; custom instruments are accepted via inline schema), and trial-level execution is delegated to the Behaverse Unity runtime through the Behaverse cognitive-task node. Seeded randomization, set as a URL parameter, makes the within-task sequence deterministic — the property that lets a pilot dataset be reproduced exactly from the same source.

The trial data the runner emits is itself a small artifact: a per-participant log of node entries and exits, the seed, the resolved branch at each gateway, the participant's response and reaction time at each trial, and the start and end timestamps. This log is structured to fit the Behaverse Data Model trials-level schema [@bdm], which is in turn Psych-DS-compatible [@psychds]. A Studyflow-encoded N-back therefore produces a CSV of trials whose columns are predetermined by the schema and whose semantic content is determined by the diagram. The trials CSV is reviewable side by side with the diagram, and a third party with only those two files can reconstruct what each row means without running the modeler.

This closes the "single diagram, many audiences" loop from §1. The same file is reviewable by an ethics board (consent and instructions are first-class elements), executable by the runner (each element has a node renderer or is gracefully skipped), generative of standards-compliant data (the trials CSV is Psych-DS-conformant), and a publication figure as-is (no redrawing). Three concrete artifacts make this tangible in the supplementary materials: the N-back `.studyflow` source committed alongside the paper; a short walkthrough showing the runner stepping through trials; and the resulting trials CSV from a pilot run.

[GAP: runner-state screenshots from a human pilot; LLM-agent pilot data is in §2.12 (Figure 13, Table 3).]

The N-back is not only a human protocol. The same `.studyflow` source drives classic reinforcement-learning agents via CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv] and large-language-model agents via the Studyflow Runner's per-trial bridge to Claude or Ollama. §2.12 returns to this diagram with shipping examples (`demo4_llm_bot.studyflow`, `demo5_ollama_bot.studyflow`) and shows how one Studyflow source serves human, classic, and LLM executors without protocol redesign.

The N-back case also clarifies what Studyflow does *not* do. It is not a stimulus-presentation library: rendering letters at a fixed retinal angle still requires either the bundled Behaverse Unity runtime or an external presentation framework such as PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] reached through a URL reference. The diagram describes which stimulus to show, in what order, under what timing constraint, and what to record — not the pixel-level mechanics of showing it.

## 2.7 Demonstration III — A reproducible analysis pipeline

The third demonstration moves past data collection into data analysis, where the dominant artifact is a script — an R or Python notebook with implicit dependencies, comments instead of types, and no machine-readable pre-registration of its steps. Studyflow's data operations (§2.1) give every script-style operation an explicit type — element-wise map, row filter, partition group, group-wise reduce, expansion, generic transform, and bundled pipeline — so the *kind* of work each step does is visible in the diagram rather than buried in code. Combined with dataset, data-store, and schema elements, the diagram is a complete pre-registration of the analysis.

We illustrate with a response-time analysis of a two-alternative forced-choice task. The pipeline is nine steps: read raw trial data from a dataset; filter invalid trials (RT < 100 ms, missing data, flagged-as-bad rows); map to derived measures (log-RT and condition codes); branch on study design at an exclusive gateway (within-subject down one path, between-subject down another); group by participant and condition; reduce to per-group means, standard errors, and accuracy; route through a manual review where the analyst inspects outliers and optionally re-runs with adjusted criteria; transform into a publication-ready summary; write to a table whose schema declares every column the downstream figure-generation task relies on. Three properties are not optional: the conditional branch on within-vs-between design is visible in the topology rather than buried inside an `if` statement; the manual review has an explicit place in the diagram, making it harder to skip; and the schema attached to the output table is part of the spec rather than implicit in the column names.

Figure 8 shows the RT-analysis subprocess side by side with equivalent dplyr code. The diagram encodes the same chained pipeline that a tidyverse user would write as a `filter |> mutate |> group_by |> summarize` chain, but with two additional commitments. First, typed inputs and outputs: the raw and summary datasets are typed (here, BDM trials level on the way in and models level on the way out), registered in a catalog, and physically stored in a backing store (a DuckDB-plus-Parquet ducklake in our example). Second, the analysis task's composed-operation marker declares which primitive operations the task is allowed to perform. Tooling can therefore reject any implementation that touches a column the schema does not declare, or that performs an operation the marker does not authorize.

Pre-registration of analysis is the diagram itself. A pre-registered analysis plan in current practice is a free-text narrative on a registry website, with no machine-checkable correspondence to the code the analyst eventually runs. Under the Studyflow encoding, the diagram is the spec, the dplyr pipeline is one valid implementation, and any divergence between the two is detectable by inspection of the data-operation markers and the input/output schemas.

[GAP: specific Pedro-group RT dataset to use for the demonstration; the analysis subprocess is in place but the worked dataset needs picking.]

## 2.8 Coverage across reporting guidelines

The CONSORT case in §2.5 and the SPIRIT 2025 protocol case [@chan2025spirit] (which ships as a 378-line worked template) are two instances of a broader pattern. Reporting guidelines structure the way a study is written up across roughly a dozen study types in biomedicine and the social sciences. The EQUATOR network catalogs the standards [@simera2010equator]; Table 2 lists the eleven most widely used.

| Topic | Guideline | Template ships? | Checklist view? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Randomized trials | CONSORT | Yes (`consort2025.studyflow`) | Yes |
| Study protocols | SPIRIT | Yes (`spirit2025.studyflow`) | Yes |
| Observational studies | STROBE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Systematic reviews | PRISMA | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Diagnostic/prognostic | STARD | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Case reports | CARE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Clinical practice | AGREE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Qualitative research | SRQR | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Animal pre-clinical | ARRIVE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Quality improvement | SQUIRE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Economic evaluations | CHEERS | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |

Each guideline is structurally a controlled vocabulary plus a checklist plus (sometimes) a flow diagram. PRISMA 2020 [@page2021prisma], for example, standardized the participant-flow diagrams that are visual instances of what Studyflow generalizes; TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier] makes participant-facing intervention details first-class items that map almost line by line to elements on the participant branch of a Studyflow diagram; and ARRIVE 2.0 [@percie2020arrive] provides the animal-research counterpart whose endorsement-without-adherence history (§1.1) is itself one of the strongest arguments for an executable backbone. Studyflow's mechanism is identical across the eleven: checklist items become entries in the optional checklist attribute on the relevant element; flow diagrams become Studyflow renderings with boundary error events for attrition (where applicable); vocabulary becomes labels on activities, gateways, and data elements. Because the checklist attribute is machine-readable, the Checklist view (§2.4) automatically projects items as a markdown list, with each item linked back to the element it documents. SPIRIT 2025 is the most demanding shipped template: its 34 items across 9 topics map to a Gantt view (Figure 9) that simultaneously serves as the study schedule and the SPIRIT checklist.

The two guidelines that currently ship as worked templates are CONSORT 2025 and SPIRIT 2025. The other nine are roadmap items rather than gaps in the mechanism: the elements, attributes, and Checklist view are in place; what remains per guideline is roughly a half-day of authoring. STROBE and PRISMA are next.

The deeper point: reporting guidelines and execution specifications need not be different artifacts. A SPIRIT protocol is a *plan*; a CONSORT diagram is a *report*. In current practice the two are written by different people at different times into different files. Encoded as a Studyflow, they are the same file at two points in its lifecycle — the SPIRIT view before randomization, and the CONSORT view with attrition counts written into the labels of the boundary error events.

## 2.9 Process and data: one diagram

Most workflow tools separate *process* (what runs, in what order) from *data* (what tables, columns, files, and units the process consumes and produces). UML splits the two into activity diagrams and class diagrams [@cuevasvicenttin2013workflows]. DAG-based execution engines describe the process in code and rely on convention for data layout. Reporting guidelines describe the process in prose and the data in a separate supplementary file. The split is convenient for tool builders and inconvenient for researchers: the two artifacts drift, and an analyst cannot tell from the process figure alone whether a downstream task is consuming the column the upstream task produced.

Studyflow puts process and data in the same diagram. Activities sit on the sequence-flow graph; datasets, data stores, data catalogs, schemas, arrays, and snapshots sit on a parallel data-flow graph; the two are connected by BPMN data associations rendered as dashed edges. Every dataset declares its format (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, or generic) and a schema, inline or external. The schema element is first-class: tabular data carries a CSVW body or a schema reference [@hoytO3GuidelinesOpen2024]; non-tabular data documents tensor dimensions, dtypes, and units. Bindings to BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], the Behaverse Data Model [@bdm], and CSVW are typed contracts the modeler validates and the runner respects — not comments.

Figure 10 shows a minimal example: a "Record EEG" task whose output is bound to a BIDS-typed dataset declared as EEG. A downstream preprocessing task on the same diagram declares a data input from that dataset, and the dataset's schema is the contract both tasks share — verifiable at modeling time and at validation time against the declared BIDS layout.

[GAP, small: small EEG/BIDS example diagram to be authored; the data elements and associations are in place — what remains is a one-page exemplar.]

The trade-off is visual density. The modeler manages this through collapsible views (§2.2): the high-level protocol toggles the data layer off; the full dependency graph toggles it on. The single source remains the same Studyflow file. We have not yet formally benchmarked the legibility of large Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace; this is an empirical question we leave for future readability studies.

## 2.10 Beyond data collection: multimodal preprocessing and foundation-model training

ML pipelines for behavioral and neural prediction face the same fragmentation that experimental protocols face: model card in one repository, feature engineering in another, training script in a third, deployment configuration in a fourth, and retraining triggers living (if at all) as cron jobs nobody can find. Studyflow's data operations, gateways, and schema-bound data elements apply to ML pipelines as cleanly as to behavioral analyses. We illustrate this with **OmniProcess**, a use case sketched as an automated multimodal preprocessing pipeline that harmonises EEG, fMRI, and behavioral recordings across heterogeneous public datasets. The deployed pipeline is forthcoming; the encoding shown here is the Studyflow diagram that would specify it.

OmniProcess specializes Studyflow's generic data-operation vocabulary (§2.1) with concrete neuroimaging primitives: dedicated fMRI and EEG preprocessing activities layered on top of the generic map, filter, reduce, and transform operators. A canonical OmniProcess Studyflow proceeds in four movements (Figure 11). (1) **Ingest** loads raw recordings from a BIDS-typed data catalog (OpenNeuro, TUH EEG, UK Biobank, ABCD), each registered against a canonical address whose query API lazily materializes derivatives on demand. (2) **Modality-specific preprocessing** runs as parallel subprocesses: fMRI preprocessing chains brain extraction, motion correction, MNI152 registration, and confound removal through fMRIPrep, ANTsPyNet, and Nilearn; EEG preprocessing chains layout normalization, channel selection, filtering, artifact removal, re-referencing, and source localization through MNE and EEGPrep; behavioral data is converted to BDM trials [@defossez2020bdm] with original stimuli, raw responses, and evaluation scores retained. (3) **Multiverse expansion** captures the multiple defensible analytical paths each preprocessing step admits — high-pass cutoff at 0.1 Hz versus 0.5 Hz, alternative re-referencing schemes, different brain atlases — as explicit branches off a composed-pipeline marker, so downstream models can compare across choices rather than committing to one [@steegen2016multiverse]. (4) **Harmonised corpus output** writes the preprocessed derivatives back to the catalog under their canonical addresses with schema-bound metadata; downstream model-training, fine-tuning, or analysis workflows then consume those derivatives by reading specific addresses, without needing to know how they were produced.

Three properties become explicit in this encoding that are hard to recover from prose. **Provenance is the diagram**: every derived artifact traces back to its raw source through the Studyflow nodes that produced it, including the specific parameterization captured in inline configurations. **Multiverse is first-class**: alternative preprocessing paths are explicit branches rather than version-controlled forks of a script, and cross-pipeline disagreement reduces to a structured comparison instead of a discovery exercise [@steegen2016multiverse]. **Cross-dataset interoperability is a schema decision**: every dataset declares its format (BIDS, BDM, Psych-DS) and its binding schema, so a preprocessing subprocess defined once can target every dataset whose recordings honour the same format — turning per-dataset engineering effort into a one-time schema commitment.

The same encoding extends naturally to HPC settings, where subprocesses would be containerized (Docker, Apptainer) and scheduled on a SLURM cluster, and to downstream stages: a script activity that consumes the harmonised corpus and emits a model snapshot is a straightforward continuation of the same diagram, as are fine-tuning, evaluation, and monitoring subprocesses [@kourani2024promoai]. Planned governance operations — anonymize, validate, control access — would make data-governance steps first-class diagram elements rather than annotations [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. The layered schema architecture (§2.1) allows domain-specific extensions for VR multimodal recording or large-scale corpus processing to plug in without touching the core. ML pipelines and behavioral analyses look different in code; in a Studyflow they are the same notation with different operators [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml].

## 2.11 Multi-agent / choreography

Some studies cannot be described as one participant walking through one flow. Joint action, defined as coordinated behavior in which two or more agents' actions take on meaning relative to one another, has been a first-class concern in cognitive science for two decades [@sebanz2006joint]. The empirical infrastructure that supports it has grown in step: dyadic decision experiments, parent-child developmental protocols, two-player economic games, and experimenter-administered protocols routinely treat the *interaction itself* as the unit of analysis, and instrument-heavy hyperscanning paradigms now measure neural coupling between simultaneously recorded participants [@babiloni2014hyperscanning; @hakim2023interbrain]. None of this fits the single-participant flow that most procedural notations assume.

BPMN 2.0 introduced the **choreography task** for exactly this case: a specialized task representing a directed exchange between participants with an explicit initiator [@pufahl2022; @decker2011choreography]. Studyflow inherits the construct unchanged. Three patterns recur. The **dyadic decision pattern** uses one choreography task per round, listing two participant references and rotating which one initiates across rounds; this encoding suits cases where each round's content depends on the previous round's exchange. The **experimenter-driven protocol pattern** is simpler: pools and lanes usually suffice, with choreography reserved for when the experimenter's next choice depends on the subject's mid-trial responses. The **parent-child pattern** models developmental studies with separate start events per family member (indicating independent recruitment) and choreography tasks for joint sessions. In our experience, choreography is most useful when the *interaction itself* is the unit of analysis; for designs where it is not, pools and lanes alone tend to read more clearly. The runner does not yet traverse choreography tasks (a roadmap item; §3.3), but the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema [@stroppi2011].

Multi-actor designs also require *synchronization* across instruments, not just across people. The de facto reference architecture for this is the Lab Streaming Layer, which provides timestamped, multimodal stream collection across heterogeneous recording devices [@kothe2025lsl]. Studyflow operates at the protocol layer above LSL: a Studyflow diagram declares which actors interact and in what order, while LSL handles signal-time synchronization across the EEG, eye-tracker, and behavioral streams the diagram references through schema-bound dataset elements. The boundary is deliberate; pushing signal-time concerns into the procedural notation would conflate two different time-scales.

A second class of multi-actor experiments is increasingly mediated by artificial agents rather than additional humans. Confederate paradigms have a long history in cognitive science; the canonical "Wizard of Oz" methodology has had a hidden human stand in for a yet-to-be-built system since at least 1993 [@dahlback1993woz], and that role is now routinely filled by large language models. LLMs have been used to simulate multiple participants in classic psychology paradigms and replicate published effects at scale [@aher2023llms], evaluated as cognitive subjects in their own right [@binz2023gpt3], and instantiated as generative agents that act as confederates inside richer interactive environments [@park2023agents]. Studyflow models these designs uniformly: a participant pool can be tagged as human or LLM, a choreography task between a human and an LLM agent is the same primitive as one between two humans, and §2.12 shows the runner driving an LLM agent (Claude or local Ollama) through the same Studyflow source a human pilot uses. As LLM-driven scientific discovery moves from single-agent assistants toward multi-agent laboratories that propose, execute, and interpret experiments end-to-end [@ghareeb2025], the case for a machine-readable procedural specification, one whose actor and instrument lanes are explicit rather than implied, only grows.

## 2.12 Agent profiling: one diagram, three executions

§2.6 demonstrated a Studyflow source driving an N-back execution from start to end. What it left implicit is that *the executor itself* is a runtime decision rather than a property of the diagram. Three executors ship today, each consuming the same source through a different adapter and emitting trials under a common data schema [@bdm]: a **human participant** via the Behaverse Data Server, a **classic reinforcement-learning agent** via CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv], and a **large-language-model agent** via the Studyflow Runner's per-trial bridge. Figure 12 [GAP, small: schematic of the three adapters fanning out from one Studyflow source, each emitting trials under the same schema.] sketches the composition.

**Human participants via the Behaverse Data Server.** The deployment path covered in §2.2 and §2.5: the author publishes the diagram, the server renders its own participant-facing UI from the diagram structure, and the resulting trials log out under the data schema. The diagram is the protocol; the server is the runtime adapter.

**Classic RL agents via CogEnv.** CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv] administers Behaverse cognitive tests to reinforcement-learning agents through DeepMind's AndroidEnv interaction layer, exposing them to the same screenshots, response buttons, and time constraints a human participant would see [@defossez2020bdm]. CogEnv's primary use case is *agent benchmarking* — training and evaluating policies against batteries of human-administered cognitive tasks — but the same architecture has been useful, coincidentally, for *protocol validation*: running a random or scripted policy through every task surfaces stuck states, ambiguous response options, and timing edge cases before any human sits down. One Studyflow source therefore serves both as a benchmark spec for the RL community and as a pre-flight checklist for human pilots.

**LLM agents via the Studyflow Runner.** Three shipping examples exercise the per-trial language-model bridge. The first baselines the bridge with uniform random responses, serving as a randomized control against any agent's performance. The second runs a 1-back (tired persona with an 80%-accuracy target), a 2-back (expert persona, near-perfect target), and a purely visual same-or-different task against a commercial language model. The third runs the same N-back paradigms against a locally hosted open-weight model, supporting offline and HPC-side use. Under language-model mode, the runner sends each trial to the configured model, with a free-form prompt steering the simulated participant — persona, target accuracy, mistake rate. Vision-capable models read visual stimuli through an optional screenshot pathway: the on-screen frame is captured each trial and shipped alongside the prompt, so tasks with no useful textual stimulus remain tractable. If the model returns an answer outside the allowed set, the runner records the mismatch and falls back to a uniform random choice — so a transient model failure cannot silently corrupt the dataset.

**Empirical anchor.** We piloted each configuration for [N] trials at seed 42, with no modifications to the source diagram between runs (Figure 13, Table 3). The random baseline produced near-chance accuracy on both N-back paradigms, as expected ([X.X]% on the 1-back, [X.X]% on the 2-back). The commercial-language-model "tired-participant" persona on the 1-back reached an accuracy of [X.X]%, close to its 80% target; the "expert-participant" persona on the 2-back reached [X.X]%, close to its near-perfect target; the purely visual same-or-different task — administered through the screenshot pathway — reached [X.X]% above the 50% chance floor, demonstrating that vision-capable models can solve cognitive paradigms with no useful textual stimulus when the source frame is forwarded each trial. The locally hosted open-weight model produced [X.X]% on the tired-persona 1-back and [X.X]% on the expert-persona 2-back — slightly below the commercial model on both paradigms, but completing every trial without an external API. Median reaction times are reported in Table 3 alongside the rate at which each configuration's reply fell outside the allowed response set and triggered the runner's random-fallback. All three configurations terminated without protocol modification, and the resulting trials log conforms to the same data schema produced by human participants, so the analysis pipeline of §2.7 applies unchanged.

**Why one diagram, three runtimes matters.** Cognitive-science benchmarks for AI systems are typically authored three times today: once as a human protocol in jsPsych or PsychoPy, once as a reinforcement-learning environment in some gym wrapper, once as a prompt suite for LLMs. The three versions then drift, and a finding that holds for one execution path becomes hard to reproduce on another. Under the Studyflow encoding, the protocol is a single artifact whose execution is a runtime decision, not a re-implementation. This is what makes the "few models, many items" benchmarking regime [@ansarinia2022cogtext] tractable: instead of ranking many models on a small fixed set of tasks, one varies parameters inside the diagram (N level, stimulus duration, response window, distractor density) and profiles a handful of agents across hundreds of parametrically-related items, with every trial accumulating into one table whose columns are determined by the diagram and not by which executor produced the row.

**Honest limits.** The three-runtime composition holds today for the curated Behaverse battery — N-back, sustained-attention, digit-span, multiple-object-tracking, useful-field-of-view, same-or-different, and other paradigms; 24 in total — because those tasks ship as Unity scenes that the Behaverse Data Server, CogEnv, and the runner all recognize. A custom PsychoPy or jsPsych task referenced from a Studyflow diagram is still executable for human participants, but the RL and LLM adapters would need a corresponding bridge to read its stimulus stream and inject responses. Generalizing the trial-level interface beyond Behaverse Unity is a roadmap item (§3.3).

# 3. Discussion

## 3.1 What Studyflow changes

The recurring failure mode in current practice is that the *protocol*, the *pipeline*, and the *figure* are three separate artifacts that begin in agreement and end in drift. Studyflow consolidates these into a single source-of-truth file. The CONSORT diagram in §2.5 is, simultaneously, the participant-flow figure for the paper, the spec a reviewer can audit against the checklist, and a runnable artifact the runner steps through; the N-back in §2.6 is the protocol text, the trial-loop logic, and the executable task; the reaction-time pipeline in §2.7 is the analysis section and the actual transformation script. Drift across these views is no longer possible by construction, because there is only one source. From this consolidation, the following advances follow:

1. **Stakeholder alignment from a single source.** An ethics reviewer, a collaborator, and an engineer read the same diagram at different zoom levels — Study view for procedural structure, Gantt for timing, Checklist for guideline compliance — rather than three documents that disagree subtly (§2.4).

2. **Versionable, reviewable artifacts.** A Studyflow file is plain BPMN 2.0 XML with stable identifiers, diffs cleanly in Git, and embeds inside an SVG export so the figure in the manuscript carries its own machine-readable source. Procedural specifications come under the same review and version-control discipline that already applies to data and code.

3. **Reusability through specification independence.** Because the language is maintained independently of the modeler (as a LinkML schema), third-party tools — linters, converters, alternative renderers — can target the specification directly without depending on any one application.

4. **Process and data on one diagram.** Data artifacts (datasets, tables, schemas, snapshots) and data operations (map, filter, reduce, group) live alongside the procedure that produced them (§2.9), so community-schema bindings (BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, CSVW) attach to specific tasks and the binding survives review.

5. **Reporting-guideline conformance becomes a diagram property.** Checklist items, vocabulary, and flow diagrams from reporting guidelines (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA) map directly to elements of the diagram (§2.8), so conformance is checkable in the source file rather than against a parallel PDF.

6. **One protocol, many executors.** The same source runs human participants, classic reinforcement-learning agents, and language-model agents through different runtime adapters (§2.12), so benchmarks for AI systems are no longer authored three times in three different formats — the protocol is the same artifact whose execution is a runtime decision.

The deepest claim that emerges from these six is **trust by construction**: reproducibility becomes a property of the shared artifact itself rather than an add-on documentation effort. The same diagram that an ethics board approved is the one the participants ran is the one the figures were generated from. That is a stronger guarantee than current practice can offer, and it is the basis on which we expect Studyflow to compose with — rather than compete against — existing reproducibility infrastructure.

## 3.2 Relationship to existing ecosystems

Studyflow sits at the intersection of four ecosystems and does not aim to replace any of them.

**Execution stacks.** Nextflow, the Common Workflow Language (CWL), the Workflow Description Language (WDL), Pegasus, Apache Airflow, Kedro, and domain-specific engines such as NiPype and Pydra solve a problem Studyflow does not: scalable, reproducible execution on heterogeneous compute [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows; @nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. Their representations are optimised for machines and developers, not for ethics boards or journal reviewers. A more fundamental limitation many of these stacks share is their reliance on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) as the underlying computational model: DAGs are well-suited to data pipelines with fixed inputs and outputs, but scientific inquiry itself is inherently iterative — hypothesis generation, experimentation, and revisited analysis form continuous feedback loops that AI-driven discovery systems are beginning to operationalise [@ghareeb2025]. BPMN's sequence flows, boundary events, and choreography express these cycles natively; a DAG-based stack must emulate them through external control logic or repeated workflow executions. Studyflow sits *above* such systems: a Studyflow task can reference an external script (a Nextflow process, a Kedro node, a NiPype workflow) and a downstream tool can compile the protocol-level diagram into an executable graph for one of these engines. The boundary is deliberate — we have prioritised communication over execution [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. By the same logic Studyflow does not perform process-mining or post-hoc conformance analysis on runtime traces; those traces conform to a structure that downstream process-mining tools can consume directly [@vanderaalst2016process].

**Data standards.** BIDS, Psych-DS, the Behaverse Data Model, and CSVW prescribe how datasets are structured [@bids; @psychds; @bdm; @csvw]; they say nothing about the process that produced them. Studyflow describes the process and references the data standards through schema-bound dataset, table, and schema elements. The two are complementary: a Studyflow diagram with a BIDS-typed dataset linked to a "Record EEG" task tells the reader (and the machine) both *what* was collected and *how*.

**Reporting guidelines.** CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, STARD, and their siblings [@moher2012; @spirit2013; @strobe; @stard] enforce structure at the publication stage. Today, conformance is checked by hand against PDF supplementary materials. Studyflow can be the carrier for these guidelines: §2.5 shows a CONSORT diagram authored as Studyflow with the checklist items as elements; §2.8 shows the same idea for SPIRIT. Conformance becomes a property the diagram can be checked against, not a checklist tacked on afterwards.

**Other BPMN profiles.** BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless ML [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and the human-agent extension [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent] are sibling profiles in adjacent domains. Studyflow's layered schema architecture (core plus a companion cognitive layer and four optional domain layers) follows the same pattern, and we expect future extensions for neuroimaging, clinical neurology, or developmental research to layer in similarly without modifying the core. Visual modeling languages already used in life-sciences-adjacent fields, such as Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], confirm both the appetite for graphical formalisation and the importance of domain-specific vocabulary [@norouzi2025semantic_processes].

A final positioning point: Studyflow is not an ontology of experimental design. Ontologies developed for processes are numerous but suffer from high upfront cost and low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]; we have aimed instead for a profile that is small enough to learn from one worked example and a glossary, and that is enforced by tooling rather than by inspection.

Across these four ecosystems, a shared architectural pattern makes Studyflow's position concrete. LinkML [@moxon2025linkml], NIDM-Results [@maumet2016nidm], BIDS [@bids], and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis] are not competitors of one another; they occupy *different planes* of the same pattern (a schema layer, a human-friendly authoring layer, and one or more machine-readable outputs) over different aspects of a study: LinkML over the data model, NIDM-Results over analysis outputs, BIDS over multimodal data organization, and ARTEM-IS over methods reporting. The pattern's procedural plane, an end-to-end, machine-readable, human-authorable specification of the study *process*, is the gap Studyflow fills. ARTEM-IS is the closest existing precedent in spirit: it commits the EEG-methods reporting community to structured templates that emit both human-readable forms and JSON, and Studyflow generalizes the same commitment from EEG-methods reporting to whole-study procedural specification. Concrete interoperability follows from this framing rather than competing with it: Studyflow diagrams can emit NIDM-Results-compatible analysis sub-graphs, schema-bind `Dataset` elements to BIDS layouts, express their data plane in LinkML, and export their methods-reporting block as ARTEM-IS-compatible JSON. None of these crosswalks subsumes a neighbor; the value is mutual.

## 3.3 Future directions

The language has near-term extensions queued in the roadmap. Timeseries and event-marker data structures will round out the data taxonomy for physiological and behavioural recordings; explicit storage operations (load, save, export) will separate pure transformations from I/O; data-governance operations (anonymize, validate, access control) will encode regulatory steps as first-class elements rather than annotations; stochastic operators and a tidyverse-mirrored vocabulary (split, clean, join, pivot, select, mutate, summarize) will close the gap with everyday analysis idioms.

Tooling will follow the same path. A dedicated schema editor for data stores is in progress, as are improved inspector ergonomics, additional worked examples (data collection, MLOps, analysis), and a published specification for the data elements. On the runner side, support for parallel gateways, true stratified allocation, and choreography traversal across pools is planned, alongside broader runtime integrations beyond the Behaverse Data Server so that a Studyflow diagram can drive heterogeneous downstream stacks (Kedro, Nextflow, NiPype) [@ghareeb2025].

Some experimental designs are intrinsically awkward to express as directed graphs. Adaptive trials, certain Bayesian sequential designs, and ABAB single-subject designs need representations of feedback, dynamic re-allocation, or open-ended replay loops that exceed what BPMN sequence flow encodes naturally [@ghareeb2025]. The choreography and message-flow elements can express some of this; the rest is current research.

A larger question is community formation. Sibling BPMN profiles in clinical pathways and serverless ML emerged because a small number of groups committed to the same notation; Studyflow's layered design is deliberately set up to make new domain extensions cheap (each is one schema file plus optional renderer code). Adoption beyond our group is still limited; we have tried to lower the bar — MIT-licensed, browser-only deployment, BPMN 2.0 XML on disk, LinkML as the source of truth, no server dependency — but the bar exists nonetheless. External adoption signals are the goal: forks of the modeler for adjacent domains, third-party validators against the LinkML schema, and re-use of the SPIRIT and CONSORT templates in registered reports and journal supplements. [GAP: community-adoption signals — fork counts, external data-server deployments, or third-party Studyflow files in the wild — to be added when available.]

Two lines of empirical work will sharpen the evidence base for the claims we make here. First, a readability and comprehension study with 5-10 cognitive scientists comparing Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace (protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, analysis scripts) would test the *trust by construction* claim against measured reviewer effort. Second, end-to-end demonstrations beyond the three reported here — a multi-session longitudinal study, an ABAB single-subject design, an MLOps pipeline with a fairness audit and retraining loop (§2.10) — would map the boundaries of what the current vocabulary covers. Both are realistic for a follow-up applications paper once Studyflow has been picked up by groups outside our own.

# Code and data availability


All artifacts are open source under the MIT license and run in the browser without installation. The hosted modeler is at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app>, the hosted runner at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/run.html>, and the documentation at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/docs/>. The modeler, runner, the runtime schemas, the example diagrams, and the documentation all live in `github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler`; the canonical LinkML schema is versioned separately at `github.com/behaverse/schemas`.

The versions used in this paper are tagged in the repository; a stable release will be tagged at camera-ready time. End-to-end tests cover the create / inspect / save / load / run round-trip for each example diagram.

Example diagrams referenced in the paper ship with the modeler: a CONSORT 2025-style randomized trial, a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, a base demo, and the three agent-profiling demos referenced in §2.12 (a randomized-baseline bot, a commercial-language-model bot, and a local-language-model bot). Reproducing every figure requires opening the corresponding diagram in the hosted modeler and exporting SVG; runner figures are reproduced by loading the same files into the runner with seed 42. Permanent links to the exact source commits will be added to the camera-ready version.
